I have gathered substantial material from the approved sites. Here are the verse-by-verse notes:

## Acts 19:1–20 — Verse-by-Verse Notes

### v. 1 — Paul arrives in Ephesus and finds "some disciples"

- **"Upper country" / "interior"**: Paul travelled the inland route through Galatia and Phrygia, not the coastal road, arriving at Ephesus from the east. (Ellicott — studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/acts-19.html; Precept Austin — preceptaustin.org/acts-19-commentary)
- **"Some disciples"**: A major interpretive crux. Luke calls them "disciples" (mathētai), his normal term for believers. Verse 3 reveals they knew only John's baptism, so they were disciples of John the Baptist. Gill argues they were genuine believers because they are called disciples and had been baptised in Christ's name. Constable and MacArthur argue they were not yet Christians — Luke elsewhere uses "disciples" for followers of John (Luke 5:33; 7:18–19). (Gill — studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/acts-19.html; Constable — studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/acts-19.html; Precept Austin — preceptaustin.org/acts-19-commentary)
- Robertson suggests they were "floating followers of the Baptist who drifted into Ephesus," sincere but ignorant. (Cited at Precept Austin)

### v. 2 — "Did you receive the Holy Spirit when you believed?"

- **Translation debate**: The Greek can be read "when you believed" (so most modern translations) or "since/after you believed." The former connects Spirit-reception with conversion; the latter leaves room for a subsequent experience. Ellicott favours "when you believed," i.e. at conversion and baptism. The AG position paper argues grammatically and contextually that "after you believed" is the better reading. (Ellicott — studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/acts-19.html; AG Enrichment Journal — enrichmentjournal.ag.org)
- **What prompted the question?** Ellicott suggests Paul noticed in them "a want of spiritual gifts, perhaps also a want of the peace and joy and brightness that showed itself in others." They had outward signs of repentance and mortification, "but something was manifestly lacking for their spiritual completeness." (Ellicott)
- **"We have not even heard that there is a Holy Spirit"**: Gill notes they could not mean ignorance of the Spirit's existence — the OT and John's ministry both spoke of the Spirit. Rather, they had not heard that the Spirit had been poured out as promised, i.e. that Pentecost had happened and the age of the Spirit had arrived. They knew He was promised but not that He had been given. (Gill — studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/acts-19.html)
- Ellicott likewise explains they knew the Holy Spirit "as a name meeting them in the Sacred Books" but "did not think of that Spirit as a living and pervading presence, in which they themselves might claim a share." (Ellicott)

### v. 3 — "Into what then were you baptized?" / "The baptism of John"

- Paul's question flows logically: if they lacked the Spirit, what baptism had they received? Christian baptism was into the triune name including the Spirit. (Ellicott)
- Gill argues their reply does not mean they were baptised in John's name rather than Christ's — they had received John's baptism which was itself administered in the name of Jesus, pointing forward to Him. (Gill)
- The Cambridge Bible suggests they "may have been disciples of Apollos and have been baptized by him before his more full instruction by Aquila and Priscilla." (Cambridge Bible — biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/acts/19.htm)

### v. 4 — Paul explains John's baptism

- **"John's baptism was a baptism of repentance"**: Paul teaches that John's baptism was provisional and preparatory — it pointed people toward faith in the Coming One, Jesus. It was good but incomplete. (Enduring Word — enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-19/; Constable)
- Gill takes a different emphasis: Paul is actually showing that John's baptism and Christian baptism are essentially the same — John himself preached faith in Christ and baptised in His name. (Gill)
- Ellicott notes Hebrews 6:1–4 may be relevant here, listing "instruction about baptisms" among elementary doctrines, then describing the higher state of those "illumined" and made "partakers of the Holy Ghost." (Ellicott)

### vv. 5–6 — Re-baptism, laying on of hands, tongues and prophecy

- **Re-baptism**: This is the only explicit instance of re-baptism in the NT. The Cambridge Bible insists "no argument can be drawn from this verse for a repetition of baptism. These disciples had never received such a baptism as Christ ordained." (Cambridge Bible)
- **Laying on of hands**: Paul lays hands on them as Peter and John did with the Samaritans (Acts 8:17). The Spirit comes through an apostle, authenticating the message and the messenger. Constable notes this authenticated God's giving of the Spirit "in a town in which demonic religious activity flourished," as verses 13–19 would show. (Constable)
- **Tongues and prophecy**: They "spoke in tongues and prophesied." Ellicott notes the verbs imply continuous action — "they were speaking with tongues and prophesying." He connects this to 1 Corinthians 14 (written from Ephesus around this time), where tongues are linked with "jubilant and ecstatic praise." (Ellicott)
- The Cambridge Bible calls this "a Pentecostal outpouring" — as at Jerusalem the gift drew attention among gathered Jews, so at Ephesus the Spirit was given "in this great centre of Gentile activity that a like result might follow." (Cambridge Bible)
- Guzik (Enduring Word) notes that Paul wrote 1 and 2 Corinthians during this Ephesian stay, and 1 Corinthians has much to say about the Spirit's person and work. (Enduring Word)

### v. 7 — "About twelve men in all"

- The small number suggests this was not the entire Ephesian church but a distinct group. Ellicott thinks they were "living together as a kind of ascetic community, attending the meetings of the Church, yet not sharing the fulness of its life." (Ellicott)
- Gill suggests these twelve "seem to be the first materials of a Gospel church at Ephesus, which afterwards was very large and flourishing." (Gill)
- The Cambridge Bible cautions against speculative parallels with the twelve apostles or patriarchs: "May it not be that the 'about' was written to admonish us of the unprofitableness of such speculations?" (Cambridge Bible)

---

### v. 8 — Three months in the synagogue

- Paul followed his usual pattern: the synagogue first. Here the Jews were more tolerant than elsewhere, allowing him three months. His subject was "the kingdom of God," which in Acts is "often a shorthand expression for the whole message about Jesus Christ." (Constable; Gill)
- Ellicott notes that during this period Paul continued his daily tent-making labour (Acts 20:34), probably still with Aquila and Priscilla, while preaching on Sabbaths. (Ellicott)

### v. 9 — Withdrawal to the hall of Tyrannus

- **"Stubbornly refused to believe and publicly maligned the Way"**: Some Jews "were growing hardened and disobedient" (Ellicott's translation of the continuous-action verb). They spoke evil of "the Way" — an early name for the Christian movement. (Ellicott; Gill)
- **"The lecture hall of Tyrannus"**: Tyrannus (meaning "Tyrant," likely a nickname) was probably a philosopher or rhetorician who owned or operated a lecture hall. One ancient manuscript (Codex Bezae) adds that Paul taught there "from the fifth hour to the tenth" (11 a.m. to 4 p.m.), when the hall was otherwise unused and when people rested from work. (Enduring Word; Constable)
- Ellicott speculates Tyrannus may have been a physician (the name appears in that context in Roman records), which might explain his connection with Luke and willingness to host Paul. (Ellicott)
- Gill notes this marked a formal separation: Paul "separated the disciples" from the unbelieving synagogue, forming a distinct congregation. (Gill)

### v. 10 — Two years of teaching reaches all Asia

- Paul's daily teaching for two years equipped believers who then spread the word throughout the Roman province of Asia. Guzik notes: "By himself, there was no way that Paul could reach this region. But he could equip Christians to do the work of the ministry" (cf. Ephesians 4:11–12). (Enduring Word)
- The seven churches of Revelation 2–3 (Ephesus, Smyrna, Pergamum, Thyatira, Sardis, Philadelphia, Laodicea) likely trace their origins to this period. (Ellicott)

---

### vv. 11–12 — "Extraordinary miracles" through handkerchiefs and aprons

- **"Unusual miracles"**: The Greek is literally "not common works of power." Luke uses a term "technically used by physicians for the healing 'powers' or 'virtues' of this or that remedy" — a characteristically Lukan touch. (Ellicott)
- **Handkerchiefs and aprons**: The Greek words are Latin loanwords — *sudaria* (sweat-cloths for wiping the face) and *semicincta* (work-aprons worn by artisans). Bruce notes these were "presumably those which Paul used in his tentmaking or leather-working." (Enduring Word; Ellicott)
- **How it worked**: Ellicott explains that the cloths functioned like the hem of Jesus' garment (Matthew 9:20–21) or Peter's shadow (Acts 5:15) — as a "point of contact" releasing faith. "The two conditions of the supernatural work of healing were a Divine Power on the one hand, and Faith on the other, and any external medium might serve to strengthen the latter and bring it into contact with the former." (Ellicott)
- Guzik stresses that *God* worked these miracles (not Paul), that they were *unusual* (not normative), and that God "will stoop down to meet us even in our crude superstitions" — accommodating the magical mindset of Ephesus to reveal His superior power. Crucially: "we should not expect that God would continue to use this method to bring healing." (Enduring Word)
- Gill calls them "special miracles" — "rare and uncommon ones, and in which there was a visible display of the power of God." (Gill)

---

### vv. 13–14 — The itinerant Jewish exorcists and the seven sons of Sceva

- **"Itinerant Jewish exorcists"**: Professional exorcists who travelled from city to city using charms, spells, and incantations. Many of their formulas were said to descend from Solomon. (Ellicott; Gill)
- They tried to invoke "the Jesus whom Paul proclaims" — treating the name as a magical formula rather than acting from personal faith. (Enduring Word)
- **"Sceva, a Jewish chief priest"**: Ellicott thinks the title was likely "part of the imposture" — he called himself a chief priest to lend authority to his trade. It is unlikely a genuine chief priest's seven sons would be itinerant exorcists. (Ellicott)
- Gill notes Sceva is not in the catalogue of Jewish high priests; the Alexandrian copy reads "a priest" rather than "chief priest." (Gill)

### vv. 15–16 — The evil spirit's reply and the violent attack

- **"Jesus I know, and Paul I know; but who are you?"**: The demon uses two different Greek verbs: one for recognising Jesus' authority, the other for familiar acquaintance with Paul. The demon knows its true enemies but does not recognise these pretenders. (Ellicott)
- Guzik: "Evil spirits know who their enemies are…and they don't waste their effort knowing those who aren't a threat to them." The sons of Sceva "had no personal relationship with Jesus" — they only knew "the Jesus the pastor preaches" rather than the Jesus of their own salvation. (Enduring Word)
- The possessed man (empowered by the demon) overpowered all seven, leaving them "naked and wounded" — stripped of outer garments and beaten. Ellicott notes as "an indication of truthfulness" that the narrative does not add a miraculous healing by Paul; a fictional account would have done so. (Ellicott)

### v. 17 — Fear and honour for Jesus' name

- News spread among "both Jews and Greeks." The incident demonstrated that Jesus' name was not a charm to be used casually — it carried real power and real danger for those who misused it. (Ellicott; Enduring Word)
- "The name of the Lord Jesus was held in high honour" (magnified): Gill says believers "thought and spake the more highly of him…more strongly believed in him, and so magnified him." (Gill)

### v. 18 — Believers confess and disclose their deeds

- **"Many who had believed now came forward"**: The Sceva incident stirred the consciences of those already converted. Ellicott notes the confession was probably public (as with John the Baptist's ministry, Matthew 3:6) — "the feeling of a vague awe at this contact with the Unseen…roused conscience into intense activity." (Ellicott)
- Guzik suggests many believers "did not know they were involved in the demonic" until this incident revealed the reality of the spiritual realm. (Enduring Word)

### v. 19 — Burning of magic books worth 50,000 drachmas

- **"Curious arts"**: The Greek (*ta perierga*) means superstitious or magical arts — soothsaying, necromancy, conjuration. Ephesus was famous for this; "Ephesian letters" (*grammata Ephesia*) were well-known magical charms written on parchment and worn as amulets. (Ellicott; Gill; Cambridge Bible)
- **Public burning**: This was significant because magical spells were thought to lose their power when their secrecy was broken. Public burning was both renunciation of the sin and destruction of its power. (Constable; Enduring Word)
- **50,000 pieces of silver**: Probably Attic drachmas. Ellicott calculates this as about £1,770 in 19th-century British coin, but in purchasing power (a drachma was a day's wage) it represents roughly 50,000 days' wages — today equivalent to several million dollars. (Ellicott; Constable; Enduring Word)
- Gill notes some manuscripts read "gold" instead of "silver," which would greatly increase the value. (Gill)
- Matthew Henry comments: "Surely if the word of God prevailed among us, many lewd, infidel, and wicked books would be burned by their possessors. Will not these Ephesian converts rise up in judgement against professors, who traffic in such works for the sake of gain?" (Matthew Henry — biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/acts/19.htm)

### v. 20 — "So the word of the Lord powerfully continued to spread and prevail"

- The verbs imply continuous, irresistible growth. The better manuscripts read "the word of the Lord" rather than "the word of God." (Ellicott; Cambridge Bible)
- Gill: the word "prevailed over conjuring books, conjurers themselves, yea, even the devils." (Gill)
- Constable identifies this as Luke's sixth "progress report," marking the end of the section covering the church's extension around the Aegean Sea (Acts 16:6–19:20). (Constable)

## Where Protestant Traditions Differ

### Are the "disciples" of vv.1–7 already Christians? (The "Second Blessing" debate)

This is the most divisive passage in the chapter across traditions.

**Pentecostal/Charismatic view**: The Assemblies of God position paper argues these men *were* already Christian "disciples" (as the term always means in Acts). Paul's question, properly translated "Did you receive the Holy Spirit *after* you believed?", assumes they believed but had not yet experienced Spirit baptism as a distinct, post-conversion event. The subsequent tongues and prophecy are the normative evidence of that "baptism in the Holy Spirit." (AG Position Paper — ag.org; AG Enrichment Journal — enrichmentjournal.ag.org)

**Reformed view (Ligonier)**: These Spirit-baptisms in Acts follow the geographical progression of Acts 1:8 (Jerusalem → Judea → Samaria → "ends of the earth"/Ephesus) and were "foundational" — given as evidence to the first-century church that the gospel was for all nations, "not meant as examples of the normal Christian experience." The epistles teach that *all* believers are baptised in one Spirit into one body (1 Corinthians 12:13), with no second-blessing category. (Ligonier — learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/when-spirit-baptism)

**Baptist/cessationist view**: MacArthur (cited in Precept Austin) argues these men were *not* Christians — they were followers of John the Baptist who had not yet believed in Jesus. "Those who insist they were already Christians use this passage as a proof text for their view that receiving the Holy Spirit is a subsequent, post-salvation, or 'second blessing,' experience. Such an interpretation, however, is untenable." Romans 8:9 makes clear that anyone without the Spirit does not belong to Christ. Constable similarly concludes they were "evidently unsaved" — John's baptism without faith in the finished work of Christ was insufficient. (Precept Austin — preceptaustin.org/acts-19-commentary; Constable — studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/acts-19.html)

**Older Baptist (Gill, 18th c.)**: Gill takes a middle ground — they *were* genuine believers who had received saving grace. Paul's question was about the *extraordinary gifts* of the Spirit (tongues, prophecy), not about the indwelling Spirit which they already possessed. (Gill)

**Enduring Word (Guzik, charismatic-leaning)**: Guzik declines to be dogmatic. "It is difficult to say with certainty if they were already Christians or not, but one can say with certainty that Paul perceived they lacked something of the Holy Spirit in their lives." He quotes Spurgeon urging self-examination: "Have ye then received the Spirit since you believed?" (Enduring Word)

### The handkerchiefs and aprons (vv.11–12) — Prosperity/WoF use

- Although no approved site directly addressed modern prosperity-gospel use of this passage, the commentaries *do* warn against treating the cloths as a permanent model. Guzik (Enduring Word) emphasises: (1) these were *unusual* miracles, (2) *God* worked them, not Paul, and (3) "we should not expect that God would continue to use this method to bring healing." Ellicott describes them as accommodations to the superstitious mindset of Ephesus, where people already trusted in amulets and charms — God met them where they were to show His superior power. (Enduring Word; Ellicott)

## Other Views

**NET Bible notes (netbible.org)**: The NET Bible (cited via classic.net.bible.org) renders verse 2 as "Did you receive the Holy Spirit when you believed?" and notes the grammatical ambiguity; the aorist participle "believed" can be temporal ("when") or antecedent ("after"). (netbible.org)

**Catholic and Orthodox views**: The search results did not yield substantial content from newadvent.org, catholic.com, or oca.org specifically on Acts 19:1–20. No distinct Catholic or Orthodox reading could be documented from the approved sites within the search limit.
